title: Diversity-weighted leaderboard and decision memo — Q2 2026 model bakeoff
body:
Executive summary:

This memo presents the results of the Q2 2026 applied-ML bakeoff using a diversity-weighted leaderboard designed to prioritize consistent behavior across prompt clusters rather than raw average accuracy. We evaluated five candidate model versions across three curated prompt families (instruction, conversational, extraction) and three stress scenarios (long-context, adversarial paraphrase, numeric reasoning).

Topline recommendation: adopt model v3.1-c as the primary rollout candidate for Hosted API with a staggered canary (10% then 50%) contingent on cost telemetry and no regression in the numeric-reasoning prompt cluster. v3.1-c leads on diversity-weighted score and shows substantially fewer high-impact failure modes in extraction tasks.

Background and motivation:

Standard aggregate metrics (macro F1, ROUGE, BLEU) favored model v4.0-b for single-task throughput; however, production logs show uneven failure modes concentrated in a small set of customer prompt families. To reduce customer-visible regressions during rollouts, we defined a diversity-weighted scoring mechanism that upweights underrepresented prompt clusters and penalizes catastrophic errors (empty responses, hallucinations flagged by verifier).

Evaluation corpus and prompt sets:

- Base corpora: internal redwood-mix-1 (prod-like user traces sampled Jan–Mar 2026), public QA/Instr (subset of OpenEval-2025), and curated extraction test-suite (financial forms, receipts).
- Prompt families (clusters): instruction (how-to, write), conversational (multi-turn chat), extraction (slot filling, entity extraction).
- Stress scenarios: long-context (>=4096 tokens), adversarial paraphrase (synthetic rewrites), numeric reasoning (tables, arithmetic).
- Each prompt in the test harness is tagged with cluster id, difficulty score (0–1), and a potential-impact label (high, medium, low) derived from product impact taxonomy.

Metrics and scoring:

Primary metrics (per-test): accuracy (where applicable), normalized-ROUGE, hallucination-rate (binary flag), response-latency (p95), cost-per-1k-tokens.

Diversity-weighted score (DWS):

DWS = sum_{clusters} w_c * cluster_score_c where w_c = base_w + alpha*(1 - cluster_coverage_c).
- base_w = 1/num_clusters (uniform baseline)
- cluster_coverage_c is model's pass-rate on cluster c relative to median among candidates
- alpha = 0.6 (experimentally chosen to emphasize undercovered clusters)
- cluster_score_c is harmonic mean(accuracy, (1 - hallucination_rate), latency_penalty) scaled to 0–100

This effectively rewards models that close gaps in weak clusters and punishes models that rely on strong performance in only one family to drive average metrics.

Execution and telemetry:

- Run dates: 2026-04-12 through 2026-04-15.
- Environment: hosted-staging with identical runtime kernels; quantization modes matched per candidate.
- Synthetic traffic replay used for burst/latency telemetry to capture p50/p95 under batching regimes (batch sizes 1, 4, 8).
- Failure classification used automated heuristics (verifier) plus manual triage for any test labeled high-impact.

Leaderboard (diversity-weighted):

Model | DWS | cluster_breakdown (instr / conv / extract) | p95 latency (ms) | cost per 1k tokens
---
v3.1-c | 86.7 | 88 / 85 / 87 | 210 | $6.20
v4.0-b | 81.2 | 92 / 73 / 78 | 195 | $7.10
v2.9-quant | 75.6 | 80 / 74 / 72 | 175 | $4.00
v3.0-rc | 70.4 | 68 / 77 / 66 | 220 | $5.50
baseline-prod (v2.6) | 62.0 | 65 / 60 / 61 | 250 | $6.00

Notes on leaderboard: v4.0-b has the highest instruction score but poor conversational robustness (multiple timeouts and collapsed context in long-context tests). v3.1-c achieves balanced per-cluster scores and lower hallucination rate on extraction items, which increases its DWS despite slightly higher p95 latency than v2.9-quant.

Win/Loss matrix (pairwise high-impact tests only):

- v3.1-c vs v4.0-b: v3.1-c wins 38, v4.0-b wins 24, ties 8. Major wins for v3.1-c are extraction slot boundary cases and numeric consistency across table-to-text conversions.
- v3.1-c vs v2.9-quant: v3.1-c wins 45, v2.9-quant wins 12, ties 13. v2.9-quant shows faster latencies but higher hallucination rates under adversarial paraphrase.
- v4.0-b vs baseline-prod: v4.0-b wins 50, baseline 4 — but high variance across conversational stress tests.

Representative regression highlights:

1) Conversational context collapse (v4.0-b): in multi-turn chats with >12 turns and intervening question prompts, v4.0-b dropped entity bindings in 18% of tests, compared with 6% for v3.1-c. This manifests as customers losing state mid-conversation.

2) Numeric rounding hallucination (v2.9-quant): under numeric reasoning prompts requiring multi-step arithmetic, v2.9-quant returned plausible but incorrect numeric outputs in 11% of cases. Manual triage found these have high product impact for reports.

3) Extraction precision improvement (v3.1-c): on receipts extraction subset, precision increased from 78% (baseline) to 90% (v3.1-c); recall improved moderately. Hallucination rate (empty-fabricated fields) reduced by 60% relative to baseline.

Risk assessment and blockers:

- Latency: v3.1-c improves quality but costs ~3–10% higher p95 compared to the cheapest candidate (v2.9-quant) depending on batch profile. If latency SLO is strict for a specific customer tier, consider a hybrid routing policy (fast-path to v2.9-quant for low-impact endpoints).
- Cost: v4.0-b is the most expensive; budget-sensitive customers may see unit-costs increase if default switched.
- Unknowns: interaction with private-deployments (on-prem quant kernels) not fully validated for v3.1-c — we observed one kernel fallback event in the staging run that needs investigation.

Rollout proposal and canary plan:

Goal: minimize customer-visible regressions while achieving quality uplift.

Phase 0 (pre-rollout): run extended nightly test harness for 72 hours focused on long-context and numeric reasoning with v3.1-c in dedicated capacity to reproduce the kernel fallback.

Phase 1 (canary 10%): route 10% of eligible traffic (non-enterprise, opt-in free-tier) to v3.1-c for 72 hours. Success criteria:
- No regression in numeric-reasoning failure rate vs baseline (>+0.5% absolute failure triggers rollback).
- p95 latency delta <= +20% on production mix.
- Cost telemetry within expected band (<+12% to historical unit cost).

Phase 2 (canary 50%): expand to 50% over 48 hours if Phase 1 passes. Monitor automated quality regressions (per-customer eval probes) and SLO budget consumption.

Phase 3 (full): rollout remainder after 7 days with no high-impact regressions.

Fallback policy: traffic should automatically fallback to baseline-prod (v2.6) under any of: sudden hallucination surge detected (>3x historical), p95 latency spike >2x, or kernel panic/fallback count >2 per hour.

Action items and owners:

- Marco Rivera: run 72h dedicated capacity reproduction and investigate kernel fallback (due 2026-04-20).
- Helen Cho: extend numeric-reasoning test cases with additional table-format variants and confirm verifier thresholds (due 2026-04-19).
- Liam O'Neill: prepare canary routing config and monitoring dashboards (SLIs/SLOs, per-cluster probes) (due 2026-04-21).
- Aisha Patel (owner): draft customer-facing rollout note and update console rollout options for hybrid routing (due 2026-04-22).

Appendix: quick troubleshooting checklist (for on-call)

- If hallucination spike observed: check model version tags, revert canary to baseline, capture 50 failing prompts into a private triage doc, notify applied-ml and product.
- If p95 latency degrades: inspect batch size distribution, kernel fallback logs, and autoscaler events. Consider temporarily lowering max batch size for canary.
- If kernel fallback repeats: collect full libcudnn/driver versions from node, escalate to infra and release-engineering.

Closing note:

This diversity-weighted leaderboard aligns evaluation with production impact by prioritizing models that reduce blindspots. v3.1-c is the recommended candidate for staged rollout given its balance of cluster-level gains and low high-impact failure rates. The proposed canary mitigations and rollback triggers are intentionally conservative to keep customer risk minimal.

Document history:
- 2026-04-12: initial run and draft results compiled.
- 2026-04-15: added manual triage notes and pairwise win/loss counts.
- 2026-04-18: updated with final DWS calculations and rollout plan.
